transcript.content: Hello. I'm Dr. Smith. To get us started, could you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, Dr. Smith, it's... it's a bit complicated, to be honest. I mean, I'm a financial advisor, right? So I deal with a lot of people, a lot of networking, especially in the arts and finance circles here in Cincinnati. It's a small world, really. You see the same faces at gallery openings, charity galas, investment seminars. But lately—well, for a while now, actually—it's gone beyond just seeing the same faces. I’ve become completely convinced that certain individuals in these groups are... tracking me. Not in a literal, following-me-down-the-street way, but they're definitely keeping tabs on which clients I'm meeting with. And it's not just that they know. They're sending me these... signals. Little messages, I guess you could call them. It happens through the most specific things, like the type of invitations I get in the mail, or the exact topics chosen for panel discussions I attend, or even—and this is the part that really gets to me—who happens to be seated next to me at these events. I've tried to rationalize it. I've sat down and told myself, over and over, that it's just a coincidence, just the nature of the business in a mid-sized city. But no matter how much I try to logic my way out of it, I just can't shake the feeling. I can't let it go. It's like this constant hum in the background of my professional life, and it's... well, it's why I'm here.
Aside from these concerns, have you experienced any periods where your mood felt significantly elevated, or conversely, periods where you felt deeply depressed for weeks at a time?

Elevated? Like... no, no, not really. I mean, sure, when the market is up and I manage to secure a really solid portfolio shift for a client, I get happy. Who wouldn't be, right? I had this one client last year where we completely restructured his retirement strategy, and I was thrilled about it for a day or two because it was a lot of hard work paying off. But not... not artificially elevated, and definitely not for weeks at a time. I don't get those massive highs. 

And as for feeling deeply depressed, no, I don't really get depressed either. I get stressed, obviously. I mean, with everything I just told you about the gallery openings and the seating arrangements, it's incredibly stressful. It takes a massive toll on you, constantly having to analyze why someone placed a specific type of invitation in my mailbox or why the keynote speaker at a seminar keeps making eye contact with me during specific financial projections. It's exhausting. But even with all that weighing on me, I still get up every single morning. I still go to the office, I still check the global markets at 6 AM sharp, I still put on my suit. I don't have those periods where I can't get out of bed or where I feel hopeless or sad. 

It's more just this... this relentless pressure from what they're doing, but my mood itself? My baseline is actually very consistent. I've always prided myself on being incredibly level-headed. You have to be in finance, you know? If you let your emotions swing around and dictate your actions, you end up losing your clients' money, and I am very, very good at my job. So no, no huge highs or deep depressions. Just... just this constant vigilance I have to maintain now.
Aside from the messages you interpret from your environment, have you ever heard voices or seen things that others could not perceive?

Voices? No, no, definitely not. I mean, I know what you're asking, Dr. Smith. You're asking if I'm... well, if I'm hallucinating, right? Like hearing people whispering in my ear when I'm alone in my office, or seeing shadows move across the boardroom wall when I'm presenting a quarterly review. No, nothing like that at all. 

My senses are perfectly fine. In fact, I'd say they're sharper than most people's, which is why I pick up on all these subtle cues at the networking events. But I don't hear disembodied voices telling me what to do or anything. When I hear someone speaking, it's because there's an actual person standing right in front of me, like a client asking about municipal bonds or a gallery curator explaining a new exhibit. And when I see things, it's the actual, physical things in the room. I see the specific embossed lettering on an invitation, or the exact placement of a chair at a gala dinner. I see reality, very clearly. 

I've never had a moment where I looked at something and someone else said, "Hey, there's nothing there." Everything I'm experiencing is happening in the real world, with real people. It's just the *meaning* behind what they're doing that's the issue. The tracking, the signals... it's all grounded in actual events. So, no, no voices, no visions. Just the reality of my situation, which is complicated enough without adding imaginary things into the mix, you know? I rely on facts and figures for a living. If I started seeing things that weren't there, I wouldn't be able to do my job, and like I said, I'm very good at my job.
Have you noticed any changes in your ability to organize your thoughts, or have others mentioned that your behavior or your way of speaking has become unusual or hard to follow?

Organize my thoughts? No, not at all. I mean, my thoughts are incredibly organized. They have to be. When you're managing portfolios, you're looking at tax implications, risk tolerance, market volatility, short-term versus long-term capital gains... you can't have disorganized thoughts. You have to be able to pull all those threads together and present a cohesive strategy to a client. And I do that every single day. 

If anything, I'd say I'm hyper-organized right now. Because not only am I keeping track of all the financial data, but I'm also cataloging all these... these interactions. Like, if I go to a gallery opening on a Thursday, I have to remember who I spoke to, what they said, what kind of hors d'oeuvres were being passed around when they said it, because sometimes the timing of these things is crucial. I have this whole mental spreadsheet going at all times. It's complex, sure, but it's not disorganized. It's actually a very intricate system I've had to develop just to keep up with what's happening.

And as for people saying I'm hard to follow? No, nobody has said that. My clients certainly haven't. I just had a two-hour meeting on Tuesday with a couple looking to set up a trust for their grandchildren, and I walked them through the entire process, step-by-step. They didn't seem confused at all. They thanked me for being so thorough. 

Now, maybe... maybe some of my colleagues or the people at these events think I'm a little more intense lately? I don't know. I mean, when I'm trying to figure out why a specific competitor just happened to mention a niche sector I was researching the night before, I might get a little focused. I might ask very specific questions to try and gauge what they know. But I'm not speaking gibberish. I'm not jumping from one random topic to another. Everything I say has a purpose, even if they don't realize what that purpose is. I'm just trying to navigate this whole situation, and I have to be very precise with my words to do that. So no, my thoughts are perfectly clear, and I communicate them exactly how I intend to.
